title: Users, licenses, profiles, permission sets, and permission-set groups
objectives: Explain that a Salesforce user needs one user license, exactly one profile, and optional permission sets or permission-set groups.
Choose a permission set or permission-set group to extend functional access instead of cloning a new profile for every job variant.
Separate user-license entitlements from profile and permission-set grants, and from roles that control record access.
Troubleshoot a missing feature by checking license, then profile, then permission set assignment—not MFA and not organization-wide defaults.
diagnostic_question: LAB_Analyst needs Delete on Lead for a two-week project. They already authenticate. Do you clone a profile, assign a permission set, change their user license, or open sharing? What would you verify first?
definition: Every Salesforce user requires one user license that sets a baseline of features. Each user has exactly one profile. Permission sets extend functional access without changing that profile and are the recommended way to manage permissions. Permission-set groups bundle permission sets for a job. Profiles and permission sets control object and field capability; roles are a different layer for record access. ([User Licenses](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.users_understanding_license_types.htm); [Permission Sets](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=perm_sets_overview.htm); [Control Who Sees What](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.security_data_access.htm))
why_it_matters: Cloning a profile for every exception creates an unmaintainable authorization catalog. Changing a user license can strip existing permission-set assignments. Interviewers listen for least-privilege permission sets, one-profile-per-user, and the refusal to use roles or sharing as a substitute for a missing license or user permission.
sixty_second_explanation: Think of a factory badge office. The employment contract is the user license: one contract per person, and it caps what tools they may ever hold. The issued uniform is the profile: everyone in that job gets one default kit. Extra keys on a ring are permission sets; a labeled ring that holds several keys is a permission-set group. Changing the contract can take the extra keys back. The org chart on the wall is the role hierarchy—it is not the uniform.
deeper_explanation: User Licenses Help: every user requires a user license. Each user can have only one user license. The license provides a baseline of access; permission-set licenses, feature licenses, and usage-based entitlements can add functionality. When you change an existing user's license, Salesforce removes currently assigned permission sets and permission-set licenses. ([User Licenses](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.users_understanding_license_types.htm))

A permission set is a collection of settings and permissions that give access to tools and functions. Permission sets extend functional access without changing profiles and are the recommended way to manage permissions. Users have only one profile but, depending on edition, can have multiple permission sets. If a permission is off in the profile but on in a permission set, the user has it. ([Permission Sets](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=perm_sets_overview.htm))

User Permissions Help recommends permission sets and permission-set groups as reusable building blocks so you avoid dozens or hundreds of profiles per job function. Enable user permissions in permission sets and custom profiles. ([User Permissions](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=admin_userperms.htm))

Control Who Sees What: permission sets, permission-set groups, and profiles provide object-level and field-level security. Roles primarily control record-level access through the role hierarchy and sharing rules. Do not treat a role as a profile. ([Control Who Sees What](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.security_data_access.htm))

To assign a permission via a permission set, the user must have a user license or permission-set license that supports it. Assignment can fail if the license cannot carry the permission. ([Manage Permission Set Assignments](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=perm_sets_assigning.htm))

mental_model.analogy: A factory badge office: employment contract = user license, uniform = profile, extra keys = permission sets, labeled key ring = permission-set group.
useful_mapping: employment contract → one user license per user
extra keys → permission sets that extend the uniform
labeled key ring → permission-set group bundling several permission sets
changing contracts takes keys back → changing a user license removes current permission-set assignments
org-chart posting → role, not a profile
where_it_breaks: A permission-set license is a purchased entitlement, not just another key on the ring.
Muting inside a permission-set group can hide a permission that is present in a bundled set; the ring is not a simple union if muting is used.
The analogy does not encode edition limits on how many permission sets a user may hold.

teach_back_prompt: Explain to a Java-security teammate why you would not clone a profile for a two-week Lead Delete need, and what happens if you change the user's license instead.

review_schedule.prompt: From memory: one user license, one profile, many permission sets, groups as bundles.
Classify: missing feature, wrong license, role confusion, sharing confusion.

Two-minute interview: profiles vs permission sets vs roles.

interview_explanation.thirty_seconds: One user license, one profile, additive permission sets, permission-set groups as job bundles. Change the license only with care because assignments can be stripped. Roles are not profiles.
interview_explanation.two_minutes: I start from entitlement: does the user license even allow the permission? Then I keep a minimum-access profile and grant overlays with permission sets or a permission-set group. I do not clone a profile for a two-week task. If the symptom is missing records, I leave this lesson for sharing. If they cannot log in, I go back to authentication.

terminology.plain: The person (or integration identity) who logs in to the org.
terminology.precise: A Salesforce user record that must be assigned a user license and a profile, and may be assigned permission sets or permission-set groups.
terminology.example: LAB_Analyst is a synthetic user with a Salesforce license and the Minimum Access profile.
terminology.non_example: A Contact record is not a Salesforce user.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Guest user: an unauthenticated Experience Cloud identity (SEC-008).
terminology.boundary: Creating users is data/identity administration; permission metadata is configuration.

terminology.plain: The purchased seat that sets the baseline of what this user may use.
terminology.precise: Each user has only one user license. It provides baseline access. Changing it removes currently assigned permission sets and permission-set licenses.
terminology.example: LAB_Analyst has a Salesforce license, not a Salesforce Platform license, because the job needs standard CRM objects the Platform license may not include. Needs verification of the exact license comparison in the target org.
terminology.non_example: A permission set is not a user license.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Permission set license: add-on entitlement for a feature.
terminology.boundary: Do not recite unofficial edition matrices; inspect Company Information in the org.

terminology.plain: The one default kit of settings and permissions for the user.
terminology.precise: You can assign one profile to many users, but only one profile per user. Profiles typically follow job function.
terminology.example: LAB_Minimum_Access as the baseline profile for employees who then receive permission sets.
terminology.non_example: Assigning two profiles to one user is not supported.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Role: record-level access, not the profile kit.
terminology.boundary: Help recommends not creating dozens of profiles for each variant.

terminology.plain: An extra bundle of permissions you add without changing the profile.
terminology.precise: A collection of settings and permissions that extend functional access. If enabled here and not on the profile, the user still has the permission.
terminology.example: LAB_Delete_Leads permission set assigned to LAB_Analyst for a project.
terminology.non_example: A sharing rule is not a permission set.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Permission-set group: a bundle of permission sets.

terminology.plain: A job-shaped bundle of permission sets assigned as one unit.
terminology.precise: A grouping of permission sets so you assign a persona rather than many individual sets. Muting can reduce permissions inside the group; confirm current Help before relying on muting in an interview.
terminology.example: LAB_Sales_Operations group containing several task-sized permission sets.
terminology.non_example: A public group used in sharing is not a permission-set group.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Profile: still one per user; groups do not replace the profile.
terminology.boundary: SEC-003 owns object vs field details inside those sets.

terminology.plain: An add-on entitlement that allows certain feature permissions.
terminology.precise: Users need both the permission-set license and a permission set containing the feature permissions to use licensed functionality.
terminology.example: A feature that requires a named permission-set license before the matching permission set can be assigned. Needs verification of the specific product in the org.
terminology.non_example: The core user license is not a permission-set license.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Feature license: another add-on path mentioned in User Licenses Help.
terminology.boundary: Do not invent which products include which permission-set licenses.

interview_questions.question: How do user licenses, profiles, permission sets, and permission-set groups fit together?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: One user license as entitlement, one profile as the default kit, permission sets as additive overlays, permission-set groups as job bundles. Roles are not in that kit; they are record access.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I start with the seat: every user needs one user license, and a license change can strip current permission-set assignments. I keep profiles few and lean. I put task and feature grants in permission sets because Help says they extend access without changing the profile. When several sets always travel together, I assign a permission-set group. If the interviewer asks about missing records, I switch layers.
interview_questions.example: LAB_Analyst: Salesforce license, Minimum Access profile, LAB_Delete_Leads permission set, no extra profile clone.
tradeoffs: Few profiles vs many permission sets to govern
License flexibility vs assignment loss on change
follow_ups: Why not one profile per user?

interview_questions.question: Why not clone a profile for every exception?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Help recommends permission sets and groups as reusable blocks so you do not create dozens or hundreds of profiles. Users still have only one profile.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: Profile cloning looks fast and becomes a drift problem: every security review has to inspect dozens of near-duplicates. A permission set can be assigned, expired, and reused. I still need a sensible baseline profile. I also check that the user license can carry the permission before I promise the overlay.
interview_questions.example: Two-week Lead Delete becomes LAB_Delete_Leads, not Profile_Analyst_Plus_Delete_v3.
tradeoffs: Operational overhead of sets vs profile sprawl
Baseline profile richness vs overlay complexity
follow_ups: When is a new profile still justified?
weak_answer_warnings: Saying profiles are deprecated with no Help citation

interview_questions.question: A user lost all extra access after someone 'fixed their license.' What happened?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Changing a user license removes currently assigned permission sets and permission-set licenses. I would restore the correct license, then reassign the sets.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I treat license edits as entitlement changes, not permission tweaks. I inspect the user's current license, Company Information counts, and the User Access Summary. I re-assign only what the new license can carry. I do not open OWD. I document that this is a known Help side effect so the team stops using license swaps as a privilege knob.
interview_questions.example: LAB_Analyst moved between license types in a sandbox; LAB_Delete_Leads disappeared until reassigned.
tradeoffs: Correcting a wrong license vs disrupting overlays
Manual reassignment vs user access policies (Needs verification in org)
follow_ups: How would you test before a production license move?

interview_questions.question: Assignment of a permission set fails. Walk the diagnosis.
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: I check whether the user license or permission-set license supports the permission. Help's example is Author Apex on a Salesforce Platform user.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I read the assignment error rather than widening the profile. I compare the permission set's license field and the user's licenses. If the feature needs a permission-set license, both the license and a permission set with the feature permissions are required. I will not 'fix' it by cloning System Administrator. If they needed record access, I would have already confirmed object CRUD and left sharing for the next topics.
interview_questions.example: A Platform-licensed LAB user cannot take a permission set that includes Author Apex.
tradeoffs: Buying the right license vs reducing the permission set
follow_ups: Where is the permission set license assigned?
What is a standard permission set?
weak_answer_warnings: Granting Modify All Data to bypass the error

interview_questions.question: How do you design a permission-set-led org without ignoring profiles?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Keep a small number of lean profiles as defaults. Put job and task grants in permission sets and bundle personas as permission-set groups. Still assign exactly one profile per user.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I separate baseline from overlay. Login hours and some defaults still live on the profile (later SEC-007). Object and user permissions I prefer in sets so they compose. A sales persona might be a permission-set group. I review least privilege: a group should not be a hidden System Administrator. I keep roles out of this design conversation except to say they are not profiles.
interview_questions.example: LAB_Minimum_Access profile plus LAB_Sales_Operations permission-set group for operations analysts.
tradeoffs: Composable sets vs harder mental model for new admins
Rich baseline profile vs many required overlays
follow_ups: How do you report on assignments?

interview_questions.question: A stakeholder says 'give them the Sales role so they can export reports.' Response?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: A role does not grant report-export user permissions. I check the user license and a permission set for the feature, and I keep roles for record access.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: This is the classic layer mix. Control Who Sees What: profiles and permission sets are capability; roles are record-level. I ask whether they cannot run the feature or cannot see certain records. Feature: permission set if the license allows. Records: later sharing topics. I also refuse to clone System Administrator because they used the word role.

interview_questions.question: When would you still create a new profile?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: When a population needs a different default kit that is not a task overlay—often license-aligned defaults or login restrictions that belong on the profile—after you have ruled out a permission set.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I do not create a profile for a two-week permission. I consider a new profile when the baseline is truly different for a large population and the user license family differs, or when profile-owned settings such as login hours must differ (SEC-007). I still assign permission sets on top. I verify edition and license constraints rather than inventing limits. I never use a second profile because a user can have only one.
interview_questions.example: A lab integration user on a different license family with a dedicated lean profile, plus a narrow API permission set.
follow_ups: How do you keep the new profile lean?
weak_answer_warnings: New profile as the default answer for every request

interview_questions.question: A Java teammate says 'profile equals role equals group.' Untangle it.
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Profile is the one capability kit. Permission sets add capability. Permission-set groups bundle those sets. Roles and public groups are record-sharing principals, not capability kits.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I draw three columns: entitlement (user license), capability (profile, permission sets, groups), record reach (roles, sharing). I give the Help sentence that people confuse permission sets and profiles with roles. I add the license-change landmine. I finish with least privilege: extra keys, not a second uniform, and never a master key because naming was confusing.
